records.source: Ὅλως ἀκούεται ἐν ὑμῖν πορνεία, καὶ τοιαύτη πορνεία ἥτις οὐδὲ ἐν τοῖς ἔθνεσιν, ὥστε γυναῖκά τινα τοῦ πατρὸς ἔχειν.
records.gloss: Actually is heard among you sexual immorality, and such sexual immorality which not even among the Gentiles, so as a wife someone of the father to have.
pieces: People are actually saying that sexual immorality is going on among you, immorality of a kind that even the Gentiles do not allow: one of you is living with his father's wife.

L.1: Actually, sexual immorality is reported among you, and sexual immorality of a kind that [is] not even among the Gentiles, so that someone has [his] father's wife.

R.1: People are really saying that there is sexual sin among you. It is a kind of sin that even pagans do not allow. A man in your church is living with his stepmother as if she were his wife.

decisions.choice: actually: it is truly so, beyond doubt
decisions.reason: Ὅλως can mean "actually, really" or "generally, everywhere". Either way the report is not a rumor Paul doubts: it is widely known and true. Paul heard it, perhaps from Chloe's people (1:11) or from the visitors of 16:17.

decisions.choice: sexual immorality: sexual relations outside marriage, here a forbidden union within the family
decisions.reason: πορνεία is the general word for sexual sin, as in Colossians 3:5. It is repeated for emphasis: this is not just immorality, but immorality of a particular kind.

decisions.choice: the text without a verb: "not even among the Gentiles"
alternatives: a form with the added verb "is named": "such as is not even named among the Gentiles"
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts add a verb meaning "is named" after "Gentiles", perhaps from Ephesians 5:3; the earlier manuscripts, followed by the SBLGNT, have no verb, and the sense must be supplied ("is found", "is tolerated"). The meaning is the same. This description is from general knowledge; reviewers must check it against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: even the Gentiles: even people outside the people of God, whose morals Jews and Christians thought low, condemned this
alternatives: the nations in general, without any contrast
decisions.reason: Roman law forbade a man to marry his stepmother, even after his father's death, and Greek and Roman writers treated such a union as a scandal. Paul's point is that the church tolerates what its pagan neighbors condemn. ἔθνεσιν here means the non-Jewish world outside the church; the Corinthian believers were themselves mostly Gentiles by birth (12:2).

decisions.choice: his father's wife: most likely his stepmother, the wife of his father but not his own mother
decisions.reason: Paul does not say "his mother". "Father's wife" is the wording of Leviticus 18:8 and Deuteronomy 22:30 (23:1 in the Hebrew), which forbid a man to uncover his father's wife, and Leviticus 20:11 puts the penalty at death. Paul's command in verse 13 echoes Deuteronomy. Whether the father was dead or divorced, and why the woman herself is not addressed (perhaps she was not a believer, compare verses 12-13), is not said.

decisions.choice: has: an ongoing relationship, living with her as a wife
decisions.reason: ἔχειν is a present infinitive, and "to have" a woman was a common way of speaking of marriage or a lasting sexual relationship (7:2; Mark 6:18). The man is living in the relationship, not looking back on a past act.

decisions.choice: is living with (B, R)
decisions.reason: "Has his father's wife" can sound like ownership in English. Balanced and Readable say what the Greek means: an ongoing relationship (m6).

decisions.choice: his stepmother as if she were his wife (R); pagans (R)
decisions.reason: Readable names the relationship plainly (m5) and says "pagans" for the non-Jewish world outside the church, since "Gentiles" is church language and the point is the contrast with outsiders (m4). "A man in your church" makes clear he is one of them ("among you").

records.heading: Sexual sin the church tolerates

records.source: καὶ ὑμεῖς πεφυσιωμένοι ἐστέ, καὶ οὐχὶ μᾶλλον ἐπενθήσατε, ἵνα ἀρθῇ ἐκ μέσου ὑμῶν ὁ τὸ ἔργον τοῦτο ποιήσας;
records.gloss: And you puffed up are, and not rather you mourned, so that might be taken out of [the] midst of you the [one] the deed this having done?
pieces: And you are puffed up! Why were you not grieving instead, so that the man who did this would be removed from among you?

L.2: And are you puffed up, and did you not rather mourn, so that the one who has done this deed might be taken out of your midst?

R.2: And you are proud of yourselves! You should have been full of sorrow instead. Then you would have put the man who did this out of your church.

decisions.choice: puffed up: inflated with self-importance
decisions.reason: πεφυσιωμένοι is the verb of 4:6, 18-19: arrogance that thinks itself above correction. The perfect tense describes a settled state. Paul does not say whether they were proud in spite of the man's sin or because of it, perhaps as proof of their freedom (compare the slogan of 6:12); either way their pride kept them from dealing with it.

decisions.choice: mourn: grieve as for a death, here grief over sin in the church
decisions.reason: ἐπενθήσατε is the word for mourning the dead. Paul uses it in 2 Corinthians 12:21 for grief over church members who have not repented. Grief, not pride, was the right response to the sin of one of their members, and it would have led them to act.

decisions.choice: so that: the result such mourning should have led to, the man's removal
alternatives: a command: "Let the one who did this be removed"
decisions.reason: ἵνα most naturally gives the purpose or result of the mourning. It is sometimes read as introducing a command, but the sentence reads well as one question, as the SBLGNT punctuates it. Either way Paul wants the man removed.

decisions.choice: the one who did this: the man of verse 1
alternatives: anyone who does such a thing
decisions.reason: The masculine singular participle refers to one particular man, the one living with his father's wife. Like "this man" in 2 Corinthians 2:5-11, it needs no inclusive wording.

decisions.choice: puffed up (B); proud of yourselves (R)
decisions.reason: Literal and Balanced keep "puffed up" for this verb throughout the letter; Readable says "proud" (see docs/corinthians-terms.md).

decisions.choice: put ... out of your church
decisions.reason: Readable says what "from your midst" means: removal from the church's fellowship, as verses 5, 11 and 13 explain. The question becomes a plain statement because it expects the answer "you should have".

records.source: Ἐγὼ μὲν γάρ, ἀπὼν τῷ σώματι παρὼν δὲ τῷ πνεύματι, ἤδη κέκρικα ὡς παρὼν τὸν οὕτως τοῦτο κατεργασάμενον ἐν τῷ ὀνόματι τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ, συναχθέντων ὑμῶν καὶ τοῦ ἐμοῦ πνεύματος σὺν τῇ δυνάμει τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ, παραδοῦναι τὸν τοιοῦτον τῷ Σατανᾷ εἰς ὄλεθρον τῆς σαρκός, ἵνα τὸ πνεῦμα σωθῇ ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τοῦ κυρίου.
records.gloss: I indeed for, being absent in the body but being present in the spirit, already have judged as being present the [one] so this having done, \v 4 in the name of the Lord of us Jesus, having been gathered you and the my spirit with the power of the Lord of us Jesus, \v 5 to hand over the such [one] to Satan for destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord.
pieces: As for me, I am away in body but there in spirit, and I have already reached my verdict on the man who has done such a thing, as surely as if I were with you.
When you are gathered together in the name of our Lord Jesus, and my spirit is with you, together with the power of our Lord Jesus,
this man is to be handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, with the aim that on the day of the Lord his spirit may be saved.

L.3: For I, though absent in the body but present in the spirit, have already judged, as being present, the one who has done this in such a way.
L.4: In the name of our Lord Jesus, when you and my spirit have been gathered together with the power of our Lord Jesus,
L.5: [you are] to hand over such a one to Satan for [the] destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord.

R.3: I am not there with you in person, but my spirit is with you. I have already made my judgment about the man who did this, as though I were present.
R.4: Meet together in the name of our Lord Jesus. I will be with you in spirit, and the power of our Lord Jesus will be there too.
R.5: Then you must hand this man over to Satan. Put him out of the church, so that the sinful desires that rule him will be destroyed, and so that he himself will be saved on the day the Lord comes back.

decisions.choice: in the spirit, my spirit: Paul's own spirit, really present with the church as it meets
decisions.reason: πνεύματι is set against σώματι ("in the body"), as in Colossians 2:5. Paul means more than that he is thinking of them: when the church gathers, he counts himself present, and his judgment stands as if he were there in person. The Holy Spirit is not meant here; Paul says "my spirit" in verse 4.

decisions.choice: in the name of our Lord Jesus: goes with the gathering of the church
alternatives: with "the one who has done this", as if he claimed the Lord's name for his conduct
decisions.reason: The phrase stands between the verdict (verse 3) and the gathering, and could belong to either, or to the handing over in verse 5. Jesus promised to be present where believers gather in his name (Matthew 18:20), and the church acts here as a body under his authority. Each reading gives the action the same authority, but the Greek does not settle which words the phrase belongs to.

decisions.choice: with the power of our Lord Jesus: the Lord's power is present and at work when the church acts
alternatives: power that the church itself exercises
decisions.reason: σὺν ("with") goes with the gathering: the church, Paul's spirit and the Lord's power are all present together. The verdict is carried out by the church, but its force comes from the Lord.

decisions.choice: to hand over: the content of Paul's verdict, to be carried out by the gathered church
alternatives: Paul hands him over by himself
decisions.reason: The infinitive παραδοῦναι depends on "I have judged" in verse 3: Paul's decision is that the man be handed over. Verse 4 says this happens when the church is gathered, and verses 2, 7 and 13 tell the church itself to act.

decisions.choice: hand over to Satan: put him out of the church into the world outside, where Satan holds sway
alternatives: a curse that brings sickness or death directly
handing him to Satan for punishment without hope
decisions.reason: The church is the place where Christ rules; outside it is the realm of "the god of this age" (2 Corinthians 4:4; compare Colossians 1:13). Being put out of the fellowship (verses 2, 13) leaves the man exposed to Satan. Paul uses the same words in 1 Timothy 1:20, where the aim is that the men may learn, and in Job 2:6 God allows Satan to afflict Job but sets a limit. The aim here too is the man's rescue.

decisions.choice: destruction of the flesh: the man's sinful self, which lives for its desires, brought to an end
alternatives: suffering or death of his body
the flesh as human standards or status, as elsewhere in these chapters
decisions.reason: σαρκός here is set against "the spirit" that is to be saved, which suggests the whole person as turned toward sin (as in Galatians 5:24, "those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh"). Many read it instead as physical suffering, perhaps even death (compare 11:30, where sickness and death come as the Lord's discipline). ὄλεθρον is a strong word for ruin, which may favor the physical sense. It is not the sense "human standards" used in 1:26; here flesh is what the man's sin has made of him. The evidence is close, so a footnote gives the other reading.

decisions.choice: the spirit: the man's own spirit, the man himself as he will stand before God
alternatives: the spirit of the church, kept pure
decisions.reason: The man is the subject of the whole verse, so "the spirit" is most naturally his spirit, as "the flesh" is his flesh. Paul expects him to be saved: the discipline aims at his rescue, not his ruin (compare 2 Corinthians 2:6-8). A few read it as the church's spirit, but nothing in the verse prepares for that.

decisions.choice: "our Lord Jesus" (twice) and "the day of the Lord", as in the SBLGNT
alternatives: forms that add "Christ" after "Jesus" in verse 4
forms that add "Jesus" or "our Lord Jesus Christ" in verse 5
decisions.reason: Manuscripts differ on how fully the Lord's name is given in both verses, and later copies tend to fill out titles. The SBLGNT has the shorter forms. The meaning is not affected. This description is from general knowledge; reviewers must check it against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: the day of the Lord: the day of Jesus' coming and judgment
decisions.reason: As in 1:8, the prophets' "day of the Lord" (Amos 5:18; Joel 2:31) is the day of the Lord Jesus. Paul looks beyond the present discipline to the final judgment.

decisions.choice: for the destruction of the flesh (B)
alternatives: so that his sinful nature may be destroyed
so that his body may be destroyed
decisions.reason: Balanced does not use "by human standards", its usual wording for flesh in these letters (docs/corinthians-terms.md), because here the word means something else (m6). It keeps "flesh" so that the reader can see the contrast with "spirit" and the reading the footnote gives.

decisions.choice: Put him out of the church, so that the sinful desires that rule him will be destroyed
alternatives: hand him over to Satan to destroy his flesh
decisions.reason: Readable says what handing over to Satan meant in practice (m5) and gives the sense of "flesh" chosen in m6. That sense is uncertain, and the footnote gives the other reading.

decisions.choice: his spirit (B); he himself (R)
decisions.reason: The Greek says "the spirit"; the article points to the man's own spirit (m7). Readable says "he himself", since in English "his spirit" can sound like one part of him.

decisions.choice: Meet together ... I will be with you in spirit ... Then you must hand this man over
decisions.reason: Readable breaks the long Greek sentence into short ones and states as instructions what the Greek gives as Paul's verdict to be carried out by the gathered church (m4).

records.gloss: Not good the boasting of you.
pieces: Your pride is not a good thing.

R.6: It is not good for you to be proud like this.

decisions.choice: boasting: the pride they take in themselves, set against the sin they tolerate
decisions.reason: καύχημα can be the act of boasting or what one boasts of. Here it picks up "puffed up" in verse 2: the church's confidence in its own standing, while it lets this sin go on. Paul uses the same word in a good sense in 9:15-16 and 2 Corinthians 1:14; the problem here is what they are proud of.

decisions.choice: not good: a deliberate understatement, meaning it is wrong
decisions.reason: "Not good" says less than Paul means; the following verses show how serious it is.

decisions.choice: pride (B); be proud (R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "boasting" so the word can be traced. Balanced and Readable say "pride" here, since Paul's argument does not turn on the word itself (docs/corinthians-terms.md).

records.heading: Clear out the old yeast

records.source: οὐκ οἴδατε ὅτι μικρὰ ζύμη ὅλον τὸ φύραμα ζυμοῖ;
records.gloss: Not you know that a little leaven all the lump leavens?
pieces: Do you not realize that just a pinch of yeast makes all the dough rise?

L.6: Do you not know that a little leaven leavens all the dough?

R.6: You know that a little bit of yeast makes the whole batch of dough rise.

decisions.choice: leaven: a piece of old fermented dough kept back from the last batch and worked into the new
decisions.reason: Bread was raised with ζύμη, a lump of sour dough saved from earlier baking. A small piece spread through the whole new batch. In Jewish teaching it often stood for corruption (Matthew 16:6; Galatians 5:9), and at Passover all of it had to be cleared out (Exodus 12:15, 19).

decisions.choice: a proverb: a small evil left alone spreads through the whole community
decisions.reason: Paul uses the same saying in Galatians 5:9. Here the one man's sin, and the church's pride in tolerating it, will affect the whole church if it is not dealt with. The question expects the answer "yes, we know".

decisions.choice: yeast, makes ... rise (B, R); leaven (L)
decisions.reason: "Leaven" is little used today. Balanced and Readable say "yeast", which works the same way in the picture; Literal keeps "leaven" and the repeated verb "leavens".

decisions.choice: You know that
decisions.reason: Readable turns the question into the statement it expects.

records.source: ἐκκαθάρατε τὴν παλαιὰν ζύμην, ἵνα ἦτε νέον φύραμα, καθώς ἐστε ἄζυμοι.
records.gloss: Clean out the old leaven, so that you may be [a] new lump, just as you are unleavened.
pieces: Clear out every trace of the old yeast, so that you can be a fresh batch of dough without yeast, which is what you really are.

L.7: Clean out the old leaven, so that you may be a new lump [of dough], just as you are unleavened.

R.7: Clear out every bit of the old yeast. Then you will be like a new batch of dough with no yeast in it. And that is what you already are.

decisions.choice: clean out the old leaven: as Jewish households removed every bit of leaven before Passover
alternatives: a general call to be clean
decisions.reason: Before Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread, all leaven had to be removed from the house (Exodus 12:15, 19; 13:7). ἐκκαθάρατε means to clean out thoroughly. The old leaven is the evil Paul has described, and the pride that let it stay.

decisions.choice: become what you are: they are already unleavened, made new, and must live like it
alternatives: they are unleavened only once they have cleaned out the leaven
decisions.reason: ἐστε is a statement: they already are unleavened, a new people through Christ (verse 7b; 6:11). The command to clear out the old is based on what God has already made them. Paul often joins what believers are with what they must become (Colossians 3:3-5).

decisions.choice: every trace (B); every bit (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable bring out the thoroughness of the compound verb (m1).

decisions.choice: which is what you really are (B); that is what you already are (R)
decisions.reason: "Unleavened" is folded into "dough without yeast", and the closing clause is made a separate statement so that the point of m2 is clear.

records.source: καὶ γὰρ τὸ πάσχα ἡμῶν ἐτύθη Χριστός·
records.gloss: Also for the Passover of us was sacrificed, Christ.
pieces: For {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} has been sacrificed as our Passover lamb.

L.7: For indeed our Passover [lamb] has been sacrificed, {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}.

R.7: {{christos:Christ|The Messiah}} has been sacrificed for us, like the lamb that is killed at the Passover feast.

decisions.choice: Passover: the Passover lamb
decisions.reason: πάσχα can mean the festival or the lamb killed for it. With "was sacrificed" it means the lamb (Mark 14:12; Luke 22:7).

decisions.choice: Christ is the Passover lamb, whose death sets God's people free
decisions.reason: At the first Passover the blood of the lamb protected Israel, and God brought them out of Egypt (Exodus 12:21-27). Jesus died at Passover time, and John's Gospel presents him as the lamb whose bones were not broken (John 1:29; 19:36). Paul's logic follows the festival calendar: the lamb was killed after the leaven had been cleared out, so now that the lamb is sacrificed, there is no place for leaven.

decisions.choice: "our Passover lamb was sacrificed", as in the SBLGNT
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts add "for us" after the verb; earlier manuscripts, followed by the SBLGNT, do not have it. The meaning is close. This description is from general knowledge; reviewers must check it against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: Christ has been sacrificed as our Passover lamb (B)
alternatives: our Passover lamb has been sacrificed, Christ
decisions.reason: The Greek holds back "Christ" to the end for emphasis. Balanced puts him first so the sentence reads naturally; Readable explains the Passover lamb, and "for us" gives the sense of "our".

decisions.choice: {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} (L); {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} (B, R)
decisions.reason: Title setting.

records.source: ὥστε ἑορτάζωμεν, μὴ ἐν ζύμῃ παλαιᾷ μηδὲ ἐν ζύμῃ κακίας καὶ πονηρίας, ἀλλ’ ἐν ἀζύμοις εἰλικρινείας καὶ ἀληθείας.
records.gloss: So that let us celebrate, not with leaven old nor with leaven of malice and wickedness, but with unleavened [things] of sincerity and truth.
pieces: So let us keep the festival, not with old yeast, nor with yeast that is malice and wickedness, but with bread made without yeast: sincerity and truth.

L.8: So let us celebrate the festival, not with old leaven, nor with [the] leaven of malice and wickedness, but with [the] unleavened [bread] of sincerity and truth.

R.8: So let us keep the feast. Let us not keep it with old yeast, the yeast of wanting to hurt others and doing evil. Let us keep it with bread that has no yeast in it: pure hearts and the truth.

decisions.choice: celebrate the festival: the whole of Christian life, lived as an ongoing Passover feast
decisions.reason: ἑορτάζωμεν is a present subjunctive: let us go on keeping the feast. Since Christ the Passover lamb has been sacrificed (verse 7), the life of his people is the festival that follows, and it should have no leaven in it. Paul's subject is the church's life, not one meal or one season.

decisions.choice: malice and wickedness: the wish to harm and active evil
alternatives: two words for the same thing
decisions.reason: κακίας is ill will, the wish to hurt others, as in Colossians 3:8; πονηρίας is wickedness in action. Together they describe the old leaven of verse 7.

decisions.choice: sincerity and truth: purity of motive, with nothing mixed in, and truthfulness
decisions.reason: εἰλικρινείας is purity, being without hidden motives (2 Corinthians 1:12; 2:17). ἀληθείας here is truth lived out, honesty in life as well as word. These are the unleavened bread of the feast: life with nothing corrupt mixed in.

decisions.choice: unleavened: unleavened bread (or loaves), as at the Feast of Unleavened Bread
decisions.reason: ἀζύμοις is a plural adjective with no noun; at Passover it means the unleavened loaves (Mark 14:1).

decisions.choice: bread made without yeast (B); bread that has no yeast in it (R)
decisions.reason: Following the choice of "yeast" in verse 6, and avoiding the old word "unleavened".

decisions.choice: wanting to hurt others and doing evil; pure hearts
decisions.reason: Readable puts the vice and virtue words in everyday terms, as Colossians 3:8 does for malice, and keeps "truth", a key term.

records.source: Ἔγραψα ὑμῖν ἐν τῇ ἐπιστολῇ μὴ συναναμίγνυσθαι πόρνοις, οὐ πάντως τοῖς πόρνοις τοῦ κόσμου τούτου ἢ τοῖς πλεονέκταις καὶ ἅρπαξιν ἢ εἰδωλολάτραις, ἐπεὶ ὠφείλετε ἄρα ἐκ τοῦ κόσμου ἐξελθεῖν.
records.gloss: I wrote to you in the letter not to mix with sexually immoral, \v 10 not altogether with the sexually immoral of the world this or with the greedy and swindlers or idolaters, since you were obliged then out of the world to go out.
pieces: When I wrote to you in my earlier letter, I told you not to mix with sexually immoral people.
I did not mean the sexually immoral people of this world in general, nor the greedy and swindlers, nor idolaters. To do that, you would need to leave the world altogether.

L.9: I wrote to you in the letter not to mix with sexually immoral [people],
L.10: not altogether [meaning] the sexually immoral of this world, or the greedy and swindlers, or idolaters, since then you would be obliged to go out of the world.

R.9: In the letter I wrote you before, I told you not to spend time with people who commit sexual sins.
R.10: But I did not mean people outside the church, all the people in the world who commit sexual sins, or who are greedy and cheat others, or who worship idols. To keep away from all of them, you would have to leave the world!

decisions.choice: the letter: an earlier letter of Paul's, now lost
alternatives: this present letter, written in the same breath
decisions.reason: "I wrote to you in the letter" points to a letter the Corinthians already had. Verse 11, "but now I write", sets this one against it, and the Corinthians had misunderstood the earlier instruction. That letter has not survived. The Corinthians later wrote to Paul (7:1).

decisions.choice: mix with: keep company with, share a common life
decisions.reason: συναναμίγνυσθαι means to mingle together with others. Verse 11 shows what is meant: close fellowship in the church, including eating together. Paul did not ask the church to avoid all contact with outsiders, which would be impossible (verse 10).

decisions.choice: the world: human society outside the church, which does not know God
decisions.reason: κόσμου here is the whole social world the Corinthians lived in, with its pagan ways (1:20-21; 3:19). To leave it would mean leaving human life on earth. The church is not to judge such people (verses 12-13).

decisions.choice: the greedy and swindlers, or idolaters: people who grab more than their share, people who take by force or fraud, and worshipers of other gods
decisions.reason: πλεονέκταις are the covetous, who always want more (compare Colossians 3:5); ἅρπαξιν are those who seize what belongs to others, by robbery or by cheating. Joined by "and", the two form one group of money sins. εἰδωλολάτραις are those who worship idols, which pagan Corinth did everywhere (8:1-10; 10:14-22). The same words return in 5:11 and 6:9-10.

decisions.choice: in my earlier letter (B)
decisions.reason: Balanced makes clear that "the letter" is not this one (m1). Readable says "the letter I wrote you before".

decisions.choice: I did not mean people outside the church
alternatives: not altogether the sexually immoral of this world
decisions.reason: Readable says who "the immoral of this world" are: people outside the church (m3), set against the "brother" of verse 11.

decisions.choice: sexually immoral, greedy, swindlers, idolaters (L, B); commit sexual sins, greedy, cheat others, worship idols (R)
decisions.reason: The same English is used for these words in 5:11 so that the reader can see the lists are the same. "Fornicators" and "extortioners" are little used today; "swindlers" covers both theft and cheating.

records.heading: Judging those inside the church

records.source: νῦν δὲ ἔγραψα ὑμῖν μὴ συναναμίγνυσθαι ἐάν τις ἀδελφὸς ὀνομαζόμενος ᾖ πόρνος ἢ πλεονέκτης ἢ εἰδωλολάτρης ἢ λοίδορος ἢ μέθυσος ἢ ἅρπαξ, τῷ τοιούτῳ μηδὲ συνεσθίειν.
records.gloss: Now but I wrote to you not to mix, if anyone [a] brother being called is sexually immoral or greedy or idolater or reviler or drunkard or swindler, with the such [one] not even to eat with.
pieces: But what I am writing to you now is this: keep away from anyone who goes by the name of {{gender:brother or sister|brother}} and yet is sexually immoral, greedy, an idolater, abusive, a drunkard or a swindler. Do not even sit down to eat with such a person.

L.11: But now I write to you not to mix [with anyone], if anyone who is called a {{gender:brother or sister|brother}} is sexually immoral or greedy or an idolater or abusive or a drunkard or a swindler; with such a person not even to eat.

R.11: Now I am writing to tell you this: do not spend time with someone who is known as a fellow believer but commits sexual sins or is greedy, or who worships idols, insults people, gets drunk or cheats others. Do not even eat a meal with a person like that.

decisions.choice: now I write: Paul is writing this now, to make his meaning clear
alternatives: what I actually wrote (in the earlier letter) was this
decisions.reason: ἔγραψα has the same form as in verse 9. Letter writers could use this past tense for the letter they were writing, since it would be past when read (as in Philemon 19, 21). With "now" set against verse 9, Paul gives his instruction afresh. It may instead mean "I meant": what the earlier letter said. The instruction is the same either way.

decisions.choice: called a brother: a church member, someone known as a fellow believer
alternatives: someone falsely claiming to be a believer
decisions.reason: ὀνομαζόμενος means "named, bearing the name". Paul means anyone who belongs to the church and bears the name of brother or sister, whatever his life shows. The word is masculine, as Greek usage required for anyone, but Paul's rule applies to men and women alike.

decisions.choice: abusive: one who insults and reviles others; drunkard: one given to drunkenness
decisions.reason: λοίδορος is one who heaps abuse on others with words; μέθυσος is one who habitually gets drunk. These two are added to the list of verse 10, perhaps because they were problems in the church (compare 11:21). For the other words see 5:10.

decisions.choice: not even to eat with: no shared meals, which in that culture expressed fellowship, and so not the Lord's Supper either
decisions.reason: To eat together was a sign of acceptance and friendship (Galatians 2:12). The church's common meals included the Lord's Supper (11:20-22), so Paul's words exclude the man from the church's table. The aim, as verse 5 shows, is his repentance and rescue.

decisions.choice: {{gender:brother or sister|brother}}
decisions.reason: The rule covers any church member, women and men (m2). Readable says "fellow believer", which needs no setting.

decisions.choice: sexually immoral, greedy, idolater, abusive, drunkard, swindler (L, B); commits sexual sins, is greedy, worships idols, insults people, gets drunk, cheats others (R)
decisions.reason: The four words from verse 10 keep the same English. "Abusive" is chosen over "reviler", which is old-fashioned, and over "slanderer", which is narrower: one who speaks against others behind their backs.

records.source: τί γάρ μοι τοὺς ἔξω κρίνειν;
records.gloss: What for to me those outside to judge?
pieces: Is it my place to judge those outside?

L.12: For what [is it] to me to judge those outside?

R.12: It is not my job to judge people who are outside the church.

decisions.choice: those outside: people who do not belong to the church
alternatives: people outside a city or building
decisions.reason: "Those outside" was a Jewish way of speaking of people outside the community; Paul uses it of non-believers in 1 Thessalonians 4:12 and Colossians 4:5. Paul's discipline concerns church members only.

decisions.choice: what is it to me: it is not my business
alternatives: a real question asking for information
decisions.reason: The question expects the answer "nothing". The γάρ ("for") explains verse 11: Paul's rule was about church members, not outsiders (verse 10).

decisions.choice: outside the church; It is not my job
alternatives: For what is it to me
decisions.reason: Readable names what they are outside of and turns the question into the statement it implies.

records.source: οὐχὶ τοὺς ἔσω ὑμεῖς κρίνετε, τοὺς δὲ ἔξω ὁ θεὸς κρίνει;
records.gloss: Not those inside you judge, \v 13 those but outside the God judges?
pieces: Are not those inside the ones you are to judge,

L.12: Do you not judge those inside,

R.12: But you should judge those who are inside the church.
R.13: God judges those who are outside.

decisions.choice: you judge those inside: the church is responsible for the conduct of its own members
decisions.reason: οὐχὶ asks a question that expects "yes": it is the church's task to judge its own. Paul has just done so in verses 3-5, and he tells them to act in verse 13. He returns to the church's judging in 6:1-6.

decisions.choice: judges: God is the judge of those outside, now and at the end
alternatives: will judge: a future tense, pointing to the final judgment
decisions.reason: The Greek letters of κρίνει can be read as present ("judges") or future ("will judge"); the difference lies only in the accent, which the earliest manuscripts do not mark. The SBLGNT accents it as present. Either way God, not the church, is the judge of outsiders, and the final judgment is in view (4:5).

decisions.choice: Are not those inside the ones you are to judge, while God judges those outside? (B); statements (R)
alternatives: Do you not judge those inside, but those outside God judges?
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps the question but puts it in natural order; Readable turns it into two statements, as the question expects agreement, and names the church.

records.source: ἐξάρατε τὸν πονηρὸν ἐξ ὑμῶν αὐτῶν.
records.gloss: Remove the evil [one] out of you yourselves.
pieces: Drive out the evildoer from among you.

L.13: Drive out the evil [one] from among yourselves.

R.13: Do what the Scriptures command: "Put the evil person out from among you."

decisions.choice: a refrain from Deuteronomy, used of removing a person who has done evil from Israel
alternatives: Paul's own words, with no allusion
decisions.reason: Deuteronomy repeats this command after laws about serious sins (Deuteronomy 17:7; 19:19; 22:21, 24; 24:7), and in the Greek Old Testament it is worded almost exactly as here, with the verb in the singular. Paul makes it plural, a command to the whole church. Deuteronomy 22:30 (23:1 in the Hebrew), which forbids a man to take his father's wife, stands in the same chapter. Paul gives no formula such as "it is written"; he takes Scripture's words as his own command.

decisions.choice: the evil one: the person who has done evil, here the man of verse 1
decisions.reason: πονηρὸν with the masculine article means an evil person, as in Deuteronomy. In other places the same words can mean the devil (Matthew 13:19), but here they apply to the man living with his father's wife.

decisions.choice: drive out: remove from the community
decisions.reason: In Deuteronomy the evildoer was put to death. Paul applies the words to the church's discipline: the man is to be put out of the fellowship (verses 2, 5, 11), not harmed.

decisions.choice: Do what the Scriptures command: (R)
decisions.reason: Readable tells the reader that the words come from Scripture (m1), which a reader of the Greek Old Testament would hear. Literal and Balanced, like the Greek, give no introduction or quotation marks.

decisions.choice: the evildoer (B)
decisions.reason: "The evil one" would suggest the devil in English (m2). "Evildoer" names a person who has done evil and needs no gender setting.
